transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?
I... I've been hearing voices and seeing things that other people say aren't really there. It's been happening for over a year now, and I'm just really scared.
Have you also had times when your mood was very high or very depressed for days or weeks at a time, and if so, did those mood changes happen at the same time as the voices or visions?
No, I haven't really experienced those kinds of extreme highs or lows in my mood. I'm not really sure about that, because I've mostly just been focused on the voices and the visions.
Have these experiences affected your work, school, relationships, or daily functioning in a significant way?

Yes, they've completely taken over my life. I don't even have the motivation to do basic daily tasks anymore, and I've stopped talking to my family and friends because I just want to be alone. Nothing I used to enjoy brings me any pleasure now, so I mostly just stay in my room.
Have you also had trouble with things like speaking less, feeling emotionally flat, or having disorganized thoughts or behavior?

Yes, I feel completely flat emotionally, and I find it really hard to speak or say much of anything anymore. My thoughts also feel very disorganized, and I constantly lose my train of thought or find myself jumping between different ideas.

latest_inference.note: Previously the only candidate was Schizophrenia. The new information supports this rather than shifting away from it: the patient has had persistent hallucinations for over a year, marked functional decline, negative symptoms (flat affect, avolition, social withdrawal, anhedonia), and disorganized thinking. There is no evidence of a mood episode occurring concurrently with the psychotic symptoms, making schizoaffective disorder and bipolar-spectrum diagnoses less likely. No alternative diagnosis from the allowed list fits better than Schizophrenia.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports >1 year of hallucinations (voices and visions), marked functional decline, social withdrawal, avolition/anhedonia, flat affect, reduced speech, and disorganized thinking/behavior. They deny sustained manic or depressive episodes temporally linked to the psychotic symptoms, making schizophrenia most consistent and less supportive of schizoaffective or mood disorder with psychotic features.
